title: Matter, atoms and elements
html:
Guiding question

How can we model the particulate nature of matter?

The accepted idea that all matter is made of atoms came from experimental evidence that could only be explained if matter were made of particles. Early classical theory said all matter was earth, air, fire and water, but it had no predictive power and could not explain the great variety of compounds, so it was abandoned. Systematic study of chemical changes led to the discovery of elements that could not be broken down into simpler substances. The fact that elements combine only in fixed proportions suggested atoms existed. Processing knowledge through observation and experiment led to the modern atomic theory.

In 2021 scientists at Cornell University captured the most detailed image of atoms to date: a regular pattern of bright dots, each one an atom. That raises a good question to keep in mind through this topic: what do models show us that microscope images cannot? An image shows where atoms are; a model explains why they behave as they do.

Understandings

SectionUnderstanding
Structure 1.1.1Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
Structure 1.1.2The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.
Structure 1.1.3Temperature (in K) is a measure of average kinetic energy (Ek) of particles.
Do now: a sample contains iron filings, sand, sodium chloride and water. Classify each part, then put the separation steps in order.

Classify: iron = element; sodium chloride, NaCl = compound; sand (mostly silicon dioxide, SiO₂) = a compound (natural sand is itself a mixture of minerals); salt water = a homogeneous mixture.

Order: 1. magnet (removes the iron, which is magnetic) → 2. filtration (sand stays on the paper as residue; salt water passes through) → 3. evaporation (water leaves, salt remains).

Why filtration separates sand but not salt: sand particles are insoluble and far too large to pass through the pores of the filter paper. Dissolved salt is present as individual ions spread among the water molecules, which pass straight through.

Matter and energy

Chemistry is the study of matter and its composition. Matter is everywhere: we are made of it, consume it and are surrounded by it. Air is matter even though we cannot see it. The characteristics of matter are:

  • It is made up of particles: atoms, molecules or ions.
  • It occupies a volume in space.
  • It has a mass.
  • Its particles are in constant motion.

Energy is anything that exists but does not have these properties. Matter and energy are closely linked; energy is often seen as a property of matter, such as the ability to do work or produce heat.

Mass and energy can be converted into one another (in nuclear reactors or stars), but chemistry studies only transformations where both mass and energy are conserved. In chemical reactions the products have the same mass as the starting materials, and energy is transformed from one form to another, not created or destroyed. (Chemical reactions are introduced in Reactivity 1.1.)

ATL Thinking skillsEinstein's equation E = mc² shows mass (m) and energy (E) are interconvertible. The energy released or absorbed in chemical reactions is relatively small while the speed of light c is very large (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹), so the change in mass caused by a chemical change is negligible. This shows the importance of approximation in science: if the effect of a factor is minor, it can often be ignored in calculations without compromising the result. Question: what other examples of negligible effects have you met in chemistry? (One you will meet soon: the mass of electrons is ignored when we work out the mass of an atom.)

The atomic theory

The law of conservation of mass and the observation that some substances always combine in definite proportions led to the idea that matter is made of elements. Elements combine to form other substances but cannot be broken down chemically.

  • Hydrogen and oxygen react to form water; the mass of hydrogen and oxygen used equals the mass of water formed.
  • 1.0 g of carbon reacts with 1.33 g of oxygen to form carbon monoxide, and with 2.66 g of oxygen to form carbon dioxide (a simple 1 : 2 ratio of oxygen masses).

Elements (e.g. hydrogen, oxygen, carbon) are the primary constituents of matter and cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Definite proportions suggested that particles of one element, called atoms, combine with atoms of another element in a fixed, simple ratio, and that atoms of different elements have different masses. This and other evidence led to the atomic theory.

Atomic theory: all matter is composed of atoms. Atoms cannot be created or destroyed, but they are rearranged during chemical reactions. Physical and chemical properties of matter depend on the bonding and arrangement of these atoms. (Internal structure of atoms: Structure 1.2.)

1.0 g of carbon combines with 1.33 g of oxygen in CO and 2.66 g of oxygen in CO₂. What does the 1 : 2 ratio of oxygen masses suggest?

  1. Oxygen atoms in CO₂ are twice as heavy as those in CO
  2. Mass is not conserved when CO₂ forms
  3. Oxygen combines in whole-number units (atoms), so CO₂ contains twice as many O atoms per C atom as CO
  4. Carbon can be broken down into simpler substances

Simple whole-number ratios are exactly what you expect if matter comes in indivisible units. All oxygen atoms are alike; CO₂ simply has two per carbon atom where CO has one.

Evidence (Nature of science)Ancient atomists, including the Indian sage Uddālaka Āruni and the Greek philosophers Democritus and Leucippus, reasoned that matter was made of tiny, indivisible particles, and that changes in the natural world are due to interactions between these particles. In the 8th century BCE Āruni proposed that "particles too small to be seen mass together into the substances and objects of experience"; he called them "kana". (Āruni lived by the Ganges in what is now northern India.) In the 5th century BCE Democritus is said to have snapped a seashell into smaller and smaller parts until he had a powder of indivisible units, "atomos" ("not splittable"). Over 2000 years later John Dalton used mass conservation experiments to propose that atoms could be classified into different types, "elements", based on their masses. Scientific knowledge must be supported by verifiable evidence. Questions: what evidence was used to develop these theories? What is evidence? Is evidence shaped by our perspective?

Elements, the periodic table and chemical symbols

Everything is made of elements: pure substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. All of the elements that exist are arranged on the periodic table, in order of atomic number. The names and symbols of every element, together with a full periodic table, are in the IB Chemistry data booklet, so you never need to memorise the whole list, but being quick at recognising them saves time in exams.

Atoms and elements are represented by the same symbols of one or two letters derived from the element names, e.g. H for hydrogen (first letter), Fe for iron (from Latin ferrum). The first letter is always a capital and the second always lower case: Co is cobalt, but CO is carbon monoxide.

SymbolName
Hhydrogen
Ccarbon
Ooxygen
Nasodium
Mgmagnesium
Ssulfur
Clchlorine
Feiron

Table 1: common chemical elements.

Chemical symbols are international: a chemist in Dubai, Tokyo or Lima writes Fe for iron, so scientists can communicate without translation. The body that agrees these conventions is IUPAC, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, the world authority on standardised nomenclature for both organic and inorganic compounds. For example, IUPAC root words name organic compounds by the length of their carbon chain (Structure 3.2):

Chain lengthRootChain lengthRoot
1 Cmeth-5 Cpent-
2 Ceth-6 Chex-
3 Cprop-7 Chept-
4 Cbut-8 Coct-

Which symbol is written correctly for the element cobalt?

  1. CO
  2. Co
  3. co
  4. cO

Capital first letter, lower-case second letter. CO is a compound (carbon monoxide: one C atom and one O atom).

Elementary substances and compounds

Atoms are the smallest units of matter that still have certain chemical properties. They can exist individually but tend to combine to form chemical substances.

  • Elementary substances contain atoms of a single element, e.g. magnesium metal (only Mg atoms), sulfur (only S atoms). Some elements exist as molecules of identical atoms: H₂, O₂, N₂ and Cl₂ are all elements, even though each particle contains two atoms.
  • Chemical compounds contain atoms of two or more elements bound together by chemical forces, e.g. magnesium sulfide, MgS (Mg and S chemically bound). MgS is the chemical formula of magnesium sulfide.

Magnesium (a silvery metal), sulfur (a yellow solid) and magnesium sulfide (a white powder) look completely different: the compound has its own properties, not a blend of its elements' properties. When atoms are bonded together as a compound they are always in fixed ratios: H₂O is always 2 H atoms to 1 O atom; CO₂ is always 1 C atom to 2 O atoms.

Elements are the primary constituents of matter: they cannot be broken down chemically. A compound contains different elements bonded in a fixed ratio.

title: Compounds, mixtures and purity
html:
Structure 1.1.1 Pure substances and mixtures

Matter can be classified as a pure substance or a mixture, depending on the type of particle arrangement. Atoms can be mixed or chemically bonded together, and that single difference controls almost everything about how we separate them.

ClassDefinitionExamples
matterany substance that occupies space and has mass
pure substancehas a definite and uniform chemical composition
element (pure)composed of one kind of atommagnesium (Mg), sulfur (S)
compound (pure)two or more kinds of atoms in a fixed ratiomagnesium sulfide (MgS), water (H₂O)
mixturea combination of two or more pure substances that retain their individual properties
homogeneous mixtureuniform composition and properties throughoutsea water, metal alloy
heterogeneous mixturenon-uniform composition and varying propertiespaint, salad dressing

In particle diagrams: an element shows one kind of particle; a compound shows identical groups of bonded different atoms; a homogeneous mixture shows different particles evenly spread; a heterogeneous mixture shows different particles in separate regions (for example one type settled at the bottom).

Classify all nine boxes first, then reveal
  1. Element: separate atoms, all the same kind.
  2. Mixture of two elements: single black atoms plus diatomic molecules of a white element.
  3. Mixture of a compound and an element: black-and-white molecules plus white diatomic molecules.
  4. Compound: every particle is the same molecule, built from two different kinds of atom.
  5. Mixture of two compounds: two different kinds of molecule, each containing black and white atoms.
  6. Compound: identical molecules, each with one black and two white atoms.
  7. Element: identical diatomic molecules of one kind of atom (like O₂ or N₂).
  8. Mixture: single atoms of two elements plus a two-atom compound.
  9. Mixture of two elements: black atoms and white atoms, not bonded.

Rule of thumb: one kind of particle means a pure substance (element if that particle has only one kind of atom, compound if it has more). More than one kind of particle means a mixture.

Pure substances cannot be separated into their constituents without a chemical reaction, which changes their physical properties. Mixtures can be separated into components that keep their own physical properties.

The iron and sulfur test

The classic demonstration of the difference:

  • Iron filings mixed with sulfur powder are a mixture. The iron is still magnetic and grey, the sulfur is still yellow, and you can mix them in any proportion. A magnet pulls the iron out.
  • Heat the mixture and it glows red as the elements react to form iron(II) sulfide, FeS. This is a compound: it has a fixed 1 : 1 ratio, is not attracted to a magnet, has no sulfurous smell, and has completely different properties from both elements.
Exam tip"Explain what has changed when iron and sulfur are heated": new chemical bonds have formed between Fe and S atoms in a fixed ratio, so a new substance with new properties exists. To prove it experimentally, show that a magnet no longer separates out the iron (and that the product does not behave like either element).

Each component of a mixture keeps its physical and chemical properties. Hydrogen, H₂, is explosive and oxygen, O₂, supports combustion, and both keep these properties when mixed. Water, H₂O, is not a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen but a compound of two H atoms bonded to one O atom. Water has none of the properties of hydrogen or oxygen (not a gas at room temperature, not explosive, does not support combustion), and hydrogen and oxygen cannot be separated from it without a chemical reaction.

Splitting compounds chemically

Physical methods (filtration, distillation, chromatography, magnets) separate mixtures; they do not break the chemical bonds holding a compound together. To split a compound into its elements you need a chemical reaction. Water can be split by electrolysis in a Hofmann voltameter:

2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)

Hydrogen collects at the negative electrode (cathode) and oxygen at the positive electrode (anode), in a 2 : 1 volume ratio, matching the 2 : 1 ratio of H to O atoms in water.

Which change would separate the elements in iron(II) sulfide, FeS?

  1. Holding a magnet over the powder
  2. Dissolving it in water and filtering
  3. Fractional distillation
  4. A chemical reaction

FeS is a compound: Fe and S are chemically bonded. Only a chemical change breaks those bonds. A magnet works on the iron–sulfur mixture, not on the compound.

Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures

Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, not chemically bonded, so they can be separated by physical methods.

  • Homogeneous: particles evenly distributed; uniform composition throughout, usually in one phase (e.g. solid alloys, air, a sugar solution). Air (nitrogen, oxygen and small amounts of other gases) is homogeneous: roughly 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen wherever it is sampled.
  • Heterogeneous: particles not evenly distributed, often with visibly different phases (e.g. oil on water, soil, cereal in milk, a mixture of two solids). Natural milk is heterogeneous because the cream rises to the top.

The type and number of intermolecular forces between two substances affects which type of mixture forms and how strongly it is held together (Structure 2.2). Ethanol and water attract each other strongly, so they mix in any proportion to give a homogeneous solution. Oil molecules attract water molecules only weakly compared with how strongly water molecules attract each other, so oil and water separate into layers.

The most common homogeneous mixtures, aqueous solutions, are covered in Reactivity 3.1; metal alloys in Structure 2.4.

Alloys are mixtures

An alloy is a mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal. The different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide past each other as easily, and the alloy is usually harder and stronger than the pure metal.

AlloyMade fromUseful properties and uses
bronzecopper + tintough and corrosion-resistant; the first alloy made by humans, roughly 5500 years ago (statues, bells, ship fittings)
brasscopper + zincharder than copper but still workable (musical instruments, door fittings, taps)
aluminium alloysaluminium + small amounts of Cu, Mg, Zn and otherslow density yet strong; over 300 alloys (aircraft, armour plating)
steeliron + carbon (and/or other elements)high-carbon steel is strong but brittle; low-carbon steel is more malleable; most steels are magnetic because they are mainly iron
gold alloysgold + copper (or silver)pure gold is soft and wears easily; alloying hardens it and changes its shade. Purity is in carats: 24 carat ≈ 99.9% gold, so purity = carats ÷ 24

Alloys count as homogeneous mixtures even though they are held together by metallic bonding, because their composition can vary continuously: there is no fixed ratio as there would be in a compound (see Structure 2.3 and 2.4).

An 18 carat gold ring: what percentage of it is gold?

Purity = carats ÷ 24 = 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75, so 75% gold (the rest is usually copper and silver).
Data-based questionsA student heated two pure substances, A and B, in separate crucibles.
SubstanceBefore heatingCrucible + substance / gCrucible + contents after heating / gAfter heating
Ared colour26.12 ± 0.0226.62 ± 0.02black colour
Bgreen colour27.05 ± 0.0225.76 ± 0.02black colour
Questions: (1) calculate the change in mass for A and B; (2) state a qualitative observation; (3) explain whether the changes were physical or chemical (melting ice is physical, rusting iron is chemical); (4) discuss whether the experiment shows A and B are elements; (5) can it be concluded that both produced the same substance?

Calculate the change in mass of B (give a negative value for a loss).

Change = final − initial = 25.76 − 27.05 = −1.29 g (± 0.04 g, since the two ±0.02 g uncertainties add). For A: 26.62 − 26.12 = +0.50 g.
Answer questions 2 to 5, then reveal

(2) Qualitative observations: A changes from red to black; B changes from green to black. (3) Both changes are chemical: the colours and masses change, so new substances have formed. (4) A gained 0.50 g, so it probably combined with something from the air (oxygen); that alone does not tell us whether A is an element. B lost 1.29 g, so it decomposed into a solid and something that escaped (a gas): something that splits into simpler substances must be a compound. (5) No: two black solids are not necessarily the same substance. You would need further tests (e.g. melting point, or chemical analysis).

Using changes of state to test purity

Practical · Melting point determinationMelting point data can be used to assess purity. Pure substances have sharp melting points close to the theoretical value. Impurities lower the melting point and cause melting over a temperature range.
Skills: Tool 1 melting point determination; Inquiry 2 record relevant qualitative observations and sufficient quantitative data.
Materials: melting point apparatus; capillary tubes; two known organic solids, e.g. aspirin and salol (phenyl 2-hydroxybenzoate).
Safety: eye protection; the apparatus gets very hot; salol and aspirin are irritants and environmentally hazardous; follow the teacher's extra precautions.
Method: (1) obtain samples of two organic solids A and B; (2) put each into a separate capillary tube; (3) mix small amounts of A and B; (4) put the mixture in a third capillary tube; (5) determine the melting point of all three samples.
Questions: record the data in a suitable format; compare melting points of pure and impure substances; research structural formulas of A and B to explain their different melting points; to what extent can melting point data be used to judge the success of an organic synthesis? (Methods: Tools for chemistry chapter.)

Why does an impurity lower and broaden the melting range? Foreign particles disrupt the regular arrangement of the solid, so less energy is needed to break it down, and different regions of the sample melt at slightly different temperatures. Boiling points behave similarly: a solution boils at a higher temperature than the pure solvent and over a range.

A student's sample of aspirin melts between 128 °C and 133 °C. The literature value is 136 °C. What does this suggest?

  1. The sample is pure, because it melted
  2. The thermometer is broken, because aspirin melts at one temperature only
  3. The sample is impure: it melts below the literature value and over a range
  4. The sample is a different compound with a higher melting point

Impurities lower the melting point and spread it over a range. A pure sample would melt sharply (within about 1 °C) close to 136 °C.

title: Solutions and separation techniques
html:
Solutions: the vocabulary

Many separations depend on whether something dissolves. When a solute dissolves in a solvent, this forms a solution: a homogeneous mixture.

TermMeaning
solutethe substance that dissolves
solventthe liquid it dissolves in
solutionthe homogeneous mixture formed
soluble / insolubledoes / does not dissolve in that solvent
dissolving (solvation)the process in which solute particles separate and become surrounded by solvent particles
solubilitythe maximum mass of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent (often per 100 g water) at a stated temperature
saturatedno more solute will dissolve at that temperature
supersaturatedcontains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at that temperature (made by cooling a hot saturated solution carefully). It is unstable: a seed crystal makes the extra solute crystallise out

Picture a sugar cube dissolving. Before: sugar molecules packed in a regular solid, water molecules around it. After: the sugar molecules have spread evenly between the water molecules. No sugar has disappeared (the mass is conserved), the particles are simply too small and too spread out to see.

Solubility and temperature

For most solids, solubility increases as temperature increases. Solubility curves show this directly.

From the P, Q, R graph: how many grams of R dissolve in 100 cm³ of water at 30 °C?

Go up from 30 °C to curve R and across to the axis: about 10 g (anything from 9 to 11 g is a fair reading).

At 60 °C, which solid is most soluble?

  1. P
  2. Q
  3. R
  4. All the same

Q reaches about 100 g per 100 cm³ at 60 °C, compared with about 40 g for P and about 24 g for R. (Note that at 10 °C, P is more soluble than Q: the order changes with temperature, which is why the curves cross.)

Six-mark question: compare how the solubility of salt and sugar change with temperature
  • Both become more soluble as temperature increases, but to very different extents.
  • Sugar is far more soluble than salt at every temperature shown.
  • Sugar's solubility rises steeply and the curve gets steeper at higher temperatures: roughly 180 g per 100 cm³ at 0 °C to almost 500 g at 100 °C.
  • Salt's solubility rises only slightly: about 36 g at 0 °C to about 39 g at 100 °C, an almost flat line.
  • So cooling a hot saturated sugar solution makes a lot of sugar crystallise out; cooling salt solution gives very little. That is why salt is usually obtained by evaporating the water rather than by cooling.
Work out which compound is most and least soluble, then reveal

Mass dissolved = mass added − residue: calcium chloride 100 − 25 = 75 g; calcium hydrogencarbonate 100 − 84 = 16 g; calcium bromide 100 − 0 = 100 g (at least: it all dissolved, so its solubility could be higher still); calcium iodide 100 − 33 = 67 g.

Most soluble: calcium bromide (≥ 100 g per 100 g water). Least soluble: calcium hydrogencarbonate (16 g per 100 g water).

These are practice numbers, not real data: calcium iodide is actually very soluble, and calcium hydrogencarbonate cannot even be isolated as a solid (it exists only in solution).

Separating mixtures

Mixtures can be separated by physical means because each component has unique properties. The right method depends on the properties of the components: state, solubility, boiling point, particle size, magnetism and the intermolecular forces involved.

  • Magnet: iron and sulfur powders are separated by a magnet because iron is magnetic and sulfur is not. The compound iron(II) sulfide, FeS, is not magnetic and has no sulfurous smell; it keeps none of the properties of its components.
  • Two solids can often be separated using knowledge of intermolecular forces (Structure 2.2). Sugar dissolves in water due to intermolecular attractions between sugar and water; sand does not.

Filtration: an insoluble solid from a liquid

The sand and sugar mixture is stirred in water, the sugar dissolves, and the mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel. Sand stays on the filter paper; the sugar solution passes through. The wet sand is dried. The filtrate is the solution that passes through the filter paper. A residue is a substance that remains after evaporation, distillation, filtration or a similar process. Filtration is everywhere in daily life: coffee filters, tea bags, water purifiers.

Evaporation and crystallization: a soluble solid from a solution

The sugar solution is heated in an evaporating basin to remove water; a drop is tested on a cold tile to see if crystals form; the solution is then left for a few days for sugar crystals to form. Heating to dryness is quicker (that is evaporation), but leaving a concentrated solution to cool and crystallise slowly gives larger, purer crystals and avoids decomposing heat-sensitive solids. Slow cooling gives large crystals; fast cooling gives small ones, because many crystals start growing at once.

Recrystallization: purifying a solid

Because solubility usually rises with temperature, cooling a hot solution makes dissolved solid come back out. This purifies a solid (e.g. aspirin) when the impurities are present in smaller amounts or are more soluble: dissolve the impure solid in the minimum volume of hot solvent, filter while hot to remove insoluble impurities, cool slowly so the pure compound crystallises while soluble impurities stay in solution, then filter, wash with a little cold solvent and dry. Check purity with a melting point: a pure substance melts sharply at its literature value, while an impure one melts lower and over a range.

Why is the minimum volume of hot solvent used in recrystallization?

  1. So that the solution is saturated and as much product as possible crystallises on cooling
  2. To make the impurities crystallise first
  3. Because more solvent would raise the boiling point
  4. So that the solution cools faster

Any extra solvent keeps some product dissolved even when cold, lowering the yield. A hot saturated solution gives the most crystals on cooling, while the small amount of impurity stays dissolved.

Distillation: a liquid from a solution, or miscible liquids

Simple distillation collects the solvent from a solution: heating evaporates the water, the vapour condenses in the condenser, and pure water is collected while the dissolved solid stays behind. That answers the desert-island challenge: to get drinkable water from sea water you need to evaporate it and condense the vapour (a survival still does exactly this with sunlight and a plastic sheet).

Distillation also separates miscible liquids with different boiling points, e.g. ethanol and water. Ethanol has the lower boiling point and evaporates first. The vapour passes into a condenser, cooled by cold water flowing in at the bottom and out at the top, and condenses to liquid. The distillate (mostly ethanol) collects in a flask; water mostly stays in the distillation flask. A thermometer at the top of the flask measures the vapour temperature.

Why does cold water enter the condenser at the bottom, and where should the thermometer bulb be?

Water entering at the bottom fills the outer jacket completely, so the whole condenser is cold; water entering at the top would run straight out and leave air pockets. The thermometer bulb should sit level with the side arm, so it reads the temperature of the vapour actually leaving the flask (the boiling point of what is distilling), not the temperature of the liquid.

Paper chromatography: substances that dissolve in the same solvent

Paper chromatography separates substances such as the components of inks. The paper is spotted with the mixture on a pencil baseline and the bottom edge (below the spot) is placed in a solvent. Substances have different affinities for the solvent (mobile phase) and the paper (stationary phase). The affinity depends on the intermolecular forces of attraction between each substance and the solvent or paper. Substances that are more soluble in the solvent travel further up the paper. The pattern produced is a chromatogram. (More in Structure 2.2.)

Chromatography of mixtures works when all the substances are soluble in the same solvent; the more soluble a substance, the further it travels up the paper, and the finished picture is called a chromatogram.

Chromatography has real uses beyond ink. Run on leaf extracts, it separates the different chlorophylls and other pigments. Scientists have used it on cassava to measure how much vitamin A precursor different varieties and parts of the plant contain, which helps advise communities where vitamin A deficiency is common on which plants are best to eat (dark green leaves and yellow roots).

Two-dimensional paper chromatography: (a) a drop of mixture is put near one corner and solvent 1 moves up the paper; (b) some hours later the spots are spread along one edge; the paper is turned 90° clockwise and a different solvent (solvent 2) is used; (c) some hours later the mixture has separated into five spots, showing it contained five pure substances. The grey spot barely moves in either solvent; the purple spot moves furthest in both.

Data-based questionsUsing the 2D chromatogram: which dot had the strongest affinity for both solvent 1 and solvent 2 (purple)? Which dots had a stronger affinity for solvent 1 than solvent 2 (yellow and orange)? Which had a stronger affinity for solvent 2 than solvent 1 (pink)?

Choosing a technique

TechniqueDescriptionRemovedLeft
filtrationmixture poured through a paper filter or other porous materialliquid(s)solid(s)
dissolution (solvation)mixture added to water or an organic solventsoluble substance(s)insoluble substance(s)
crystallizationmixture dissolved in hot water or organic solvent, solution cools, crystals formed are isolated by filtrationmore soluble substance(s)less soluble substance(s)
evaporation or distillationmixture heated until one or more components vaporizevolatile liquid(s)solid(s) and/or non-volatile liquid(s)
paper chromatographymixture placed on paper; one side dipped in water or a solvent; components move along the papermore soluble component(s) move fasterless soluble component(s) move slower or stay in place

Table 3: summary of separation techniques.

Which method gives pure water from sea water?

  1. Filtration
  2. Evaporation to dryness
  3. Simple distillation
  4. Paper chromatography

The salt is dissolved, so it passes through filter paper. Evaporation keeps the salt but loses the water to the air. Distillation evaporates the water and condenses it again, so you collect it.

ActivitySuggest a method to separate: (a) salt and pepper; (b) several water-soluble dyes; (c) sugar and water; (d) iron and copper filings. Describe the technique and how each component is isolated.
Answers to the activity, plus four more from class

(a) Add water, filter off the pepper (residue), evaporate the filtrate for the salt. (b) Paper chromatography. (c) Evaporation/crystallization for the sugar, or distillation to collect the water too. (d) A magnet attracts the iron.

Copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) sulfate solution: crystallization. Pure water from sea water: distillation. Clean water from muddy water: filtration (then distillation if you need it truly pure). Sand from sand and water: filtration.

Reverse osmosis is an advanced filtration technique that removes salt from seawater, giving fresh water to millions of people; desalination (by reverse osmosis and by thermal distillation) supplies most of the UAE's drinking water. It needs vast amounts of energy, mostly from fossil fuels, so alternative energy sources matter.

Practical · Planning experiments and risk assessmentsSkills: Tool 1 separation of mixtures; Tool 1 addressing safety of self, others and the environment.
Instructions: (1) devise a method to separate a mixture of sand, salt, iron filings and powdered calcium carbonate, considering the physical and chemical properties of all four; (2) write a risk assessment: identify the hazards, assess the level of risk, decide relevant control measures, identify suitable disposal methods in line with school policy; (3) if time, try it out after your teacher validates the method and risk assessment.
Extension: weigh each component before mixing, carry out the separation, dry and reweigh each component, and calculate the percentage recovery of each.
One workable plan for the four-component mixture

(1) Magnet removes the iron. (2) Add water and stir: only the salt dissolves. Filter: the filtrate is salt solution (evaporate it to recover the salt); the residue is sand + calcium carbonate. (3) Calcium carbonate and sand are both insoluble, so a chemical step is needed: add dilute hydrochloric acid, which reacts with CaCO₃ (fizzing, CO₂ given off) but not with sand; filter off the sand. The calcium is now in solution as calcium chloride, so this step recovers the sand but not the original calcium carbonate. Percentage recovery = mass recovered ÷ mass at start × 100.

Linking questionsWhat factors are considered in choosing a method to separate the components of a mixture? (Tool 1) How can the products of a reaction be purified? (Tool 1) How do intermolecular forces influence the type of mixture that forms between two substances? (Structure 2.2) Why are alloys generally considered to be mixtures, even though they often contain metallic bonding? (Structure 2.3 and 2.4)

title: States of matter and changes of state
html:
Structure 1.1.2 Solids, liquids and gases

Matter is made of particles. The type of interactions between the particles determines the state of matter: solid, liquid or gas. All substances can exist in all three states, depending on temperature and pressure. The kinetic molecular theory explains the properties of each state in terms of how the particles are arranged and how they move.

State symbols are written in brackets after the formula: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas.

  • Water is a solid below 0 °C: H₂O(s)
  • Water is a liquid between 0 and 100 °C: H₂O(l)
  • Water is a gas above 100 °C: H₂O(g)

(aq) is used for species dissolved in water (aqueous solution). NaCl(aq) is sodium chloride dissolved in water; NaCl(s) is the pure solid compound.

PropertySolidLiquidGas
Arrangementregular, closely packedrandom, still touchingrandom, far apart
Volumefixedfixednot fixed
Shapefixednot fixednot fixed
Compressibilitycannot be compressedcannot be compressedcan be compressed
Attractive forces between particlesstrongweaker than in solidsnegligible
Particle motionvibrate in fixed positions, do not move aroundvibrate, rotate and move aroundvibrate, rotate and move around faster than in a liquid

A frozen waterfall shows all three states of water at once: ice, liquid water and water vapour (the visible "steam" is actually tiny droplets of liquid that have condensed from the invisible vapour).

Common mistakeDrawing liquid particles with gaps between them. In a liquid the particles are still touching, just randomly arranged; there is no space to squash them into, which is why liquids are almost incompressible.

Which state symbol is correct for sugar dissolved in water?

  1. (s)
  2. (l)
  3. (g)
  4. (aq)

(aq) means dissolved in water. (l) is only for a pure liquid, such as H₂O(l) or ethanol, C₂H₅OH(l).

Working out the state from melting and boiling points

Compare the temperature with the melting point (m.p.) and boiling point (b.p.):

  • T below m.p. → solid; T between m.p. and b.p. → liquid; T above b.p. → gas.
Substancem.p. / °Cb.p. / °CState at room temperature (about 25 °C)
A−100100liquid
B−1250gas
C70200solid
D1185liquid
E−80−11gas

Iron melts at 1538 °C and boils at 2862 °C. What state is iron in at 2700 °C?

  1. Solid
  2. Gas
  3. Liquid
  4. Solid and gas together

2700 °C is above the melting point but below the boiling point, so iron is liquid. (At 500 °C it is solid; at 3000 °C, gas.)

Practice: a wax melts at 37 °C and boils at 370 °C; nitrogen melts at −210 °C and boils at −196 °C; water. Predict, then reveal.
  • Wax at 40 °C: liquid (above m.p., below b.p.). At 4 °C: solid. At 400 °C: gas.
  • Nitrogen at room temperature: gas (far above its b.p.). At −196 °C: this is its boiling point (more precisely −195.8 °C), so liquid and gas can coexist; just below it, nitrogen is liquid.
  • Nitrogen at −300 °C: a trick question. No temperature can be below absolute zero, −273.15 °C, so −300 °C does not exist.
  • Water at 20 °C: liquid (between 0 and 100 °C). At 120 °C: gas. At −20 °C: solid.

Changes of state

Substances change state as they absorb or release energy. When ice is heated, its particles keep vibrating in fixed positions but more violently until the melting point is reached, and the ice melts (solid to liquid). Further heating makes the particles move faster until the water vaporizes and becomes a gas. Lowering the temperature reverses these changes. Changes of state are physical changes: they are reversible and no new substances are formed.

Sublimation: a solid turns directly into a gas without melting, e.g. dry ice, CO₂(s), used to refrigerate ice cream and biological samples. The opposite process is deposition: at low temperatures water vapour in the air solidifies directly to form snowflakes and frost.

  • More condensed state to a less condensed state (solid to liquid, solid to gas, liquid to gas): particles absorb energy from the surroundings. These are endothermic processes.
  • Less condensed state to a more condensed state (gas to liquid, gas to solid, liquid to solid): particles lose energy to the surroundings and, for a molecular substance, intermolecular forces become stronger. Releasing energy to the surroundings is an exothermic process.
ChangeFrom → toEnergy
meltingsolid → liquidendothermic
vaporization (boiling or evaporation)liquid → gasendothermic
sublimationsolid → gasendothermic
freezingliquid → solidexothermic
condensationgas → liquidexothermic
depositiongas → solidexothermic

Picture a triangle with solid, liquid and gas at the corners, joined by these six arrows: every arrow heading towards "gas" is endothermic, every arrow heading away from it is exothermic. Think of a bar of chocolate melting in your hand: it takes energy from your hand. Freezing water into ice means removing energy (the freezer does this).

Orange growers spray fruit with water on cold nights. Freezing of water is exothermic and releases energy (heat) to the fruit, protecting it from the cold.

Which change of state is exothermic?

  1. Sublimation of iodine
  2. Frost forming on a car windscreen
  3. Evaporation of sweat
  4. Melting of ice

Frost forms by deposition (gas → solid), which releases energy. The other three move to a less condensed state and absorb energy; that is why sweating cools you.

Heating and cooling curves

When water is heated there is no temperature change while solid turns to liquid or liquid turns to gas. The added energy is used to disrupt the solid lattice and to overcome the intermolecular forces between molecules in the liquid. Temperature rises for ice, then stays flat at 0 °C (ice + water, melting; freezing in reverse), rises for water, stays flat at 100 °C (water + steam, vaporization; condensation in reverse), then rises for steam.

Why the plateaus? While a substance is melting or boiling, the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the particles (they move further apart against their attractions), not their kinetic energy. Because temperature measures average kinetic energy, it does not rise until the change of state is complete. A cooling curve shows the same plateaus at the freezing and condensation points, where energy is released as attractions form. The boiling plateau is longer than the melting one, because separating liquid particles completely needs much more energy than loosening a solid into a liquid.

Common mistakeSaying that bonds "break" when a molecular substance melts or boils. The intermolecular forces are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules stay intact. Boiling water gives H₂O molecules, not hydrogen and oxygen.

Why is helium a gas at room temperature while iron is a solid? It all comes down to how strongly the particles are held together. Iron has strong metallic bonding, so a lot of energy is needed to separate the particles: it melts at 1538 °C. Helium atoms attract each other extremely weakly, so very little energy is needed to separate them: helium boils at about −269 °C, and stays a gas even at very low temperatures.

During the flat section of a heating curve at the boiling point, what is happening to the particles?

  1. Their average kinetic energy stays constant while the energy supplied overcomes the forces between them
  2. Their average kinetic energy increases
  3. Covalent bonds within molecules are breaking
  4. No energy is being absorbed

Constant temperature means constant average kinetic energy. Energy is still going in, but it is used to separate the particles (overcoming intermolecular forces), not to speed them up.

Limitations of the simple particle model

The simple model treats particles as hard, identical spheres with no forces between them. Real particles differ in size and shape (they are often not spherical), may carry charges, and attract one another. These limitations explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour (S1.5) and why substances have such different melting and boiling points (S2).

Energy changes in chemical reactions

Changes of state are not the only processes that take in or give out energy. A reaction that transfers heat energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises, is exothermic (a combustion, or an explosive demonstration such as the "cannon fire" reaction). Even such a reaction usually needs some energy put in to start it. A reaction that takes heat energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls, is endothermic. Mixing solid barium hydroxide with ammonium thiocyanate is so endothermic that a beaker standing on a few drops of water freezes onto the wooden block beneath it.

Why? Breaking bonds absorbs energy; making bonds releases energy. Every reaction does both. If more energy is released forming the new bonds than is absorbed breaking the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall; if less, it is endothermic (Reactivity 1.2).

Dilute sulfuric acid starts at 24.0 °C and reaches 31.5 °C during a reaction. Calculate the temperature change.

ΔT = 31.5 − 24.0 = +7.5 °C (the same as 7.5 K). The temperature of the surroundings rose, so the reaction is exothermic.
Practical · Non-Newtonian fluidsNon-Newtonian fluids do not behave like typical liquids: their viscosity changes with the force applied to them. You make maize starch slime ("oobleck").
Skills: Inquiry 1 identify dependent and independent variables; Inquiry 2 identify and record relevant qualitative observations.
Safety: wear eye protection.
Materials: spoon or large spatula; 250 cm³ beaker; powdered maize starch; water.
Method: (1) add three or four heaped spoons of maize starch to the beaker and note its appearance and consistency; (2) slowly add water and mix until the mixture is thick, adjusting with more starch or water; (3) explore its properties: it should harden if tapped and flow smoothly if stirred slowly.
Questions: (1) describe the properties and state of powdered maize starch, water and the starch–water mixture; (2) develop a research question about the mixture with independent and dependent variables; (3) research other non-Newtonian fluids; (4) reflect: "I used to think... Now, I think..."
Linking questionsWhy are some substances solid while others are fluid under standard conditions? (Structure 2.4) Why are some changes of state endothermic and some exothermic? (Structure 2, Reactivity 1.2)

title: Temperature and the Kelvin scale
html:
Structure 1.1.3 What is temperature?

Do now: which is the coldest object in the room, the metal table leg, the wooden desk or the plastic chair? The surprising answer: they are all at the same temperature. Metal only feels colder because it conducts energy away from your hand faster.

As temperature rises, the energies of particles increase. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. As substances absorb energy, particles in a solid vibrate more in the lattice, particles in a liquid vibrate more and move faster, and particles in a gas move faster. Temperature is measured with a thermometer (thermo = heat, meter = measure). In a liquid-in-glass thermometer the liquid in the bulb (mercury or coloured alcohol) expands as its particles move more and spread out, and is forced up the thin capillary tube against a scale.

Temperature is not the same as heat

  • Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.
  • Thermal energy (heat content) is the total kinetic energy of all the particles, so it depends on the amount of substance as well as on the temperature.
  • A cup of water at 100 °C has faster-moving particles than a bucket at 50 °C, but the bucket stores more thermal energy because it has far more particles, so it would do more to warm a swimming pool.

The teacher's poll makes the same point: would you rather have $1000 from one person, or one cent from everyone in New York? One cent each is tiny (like the low average energy of particles in a cold object), but there are more than 8 million New Yorkers, so the total is over $80 000. A huge number of slow particles can hold more energy in total than a few fast ones.

Exam question (4 marks)Which has a higher thermal energy store: an iceberg at −5 °C or a red-hot iron nail? Mark scheme: the iceberg has a lower temperature (1) but has a vastly greater number of particles (1), so collectively there is more energy among the vibrating particles (1); therefore the iceberg has the bigger thermal energy store (1). A friend who says "an iceberg is hotter than a match" is wrong about temperature, but right that it holds more thermal energy.

True or false: "A cup of water at 50 °C has a higher thermal energy store than a bucket of water at 30 °C."

  1. True, because it is hotter
  2. True, because energy cannot be destroyed
  3. False: the cup has the higher temperature, but the bucket has far more particles, so more total thermal energy
  4. False: thermal energy does not depend on temperature

Higher temperature means higher average kinetic energy. Thermal energy is a total, so it depends on how many particles there are too. (Also from the class true/false: energy cannot be destroyed, only transferred; a cup at 50 °C does have a higher temperature than a bucket at 30 °C.)

When two objects at different temperatures touch, energy flows from the hotter to the colder until they reach the same temperature: thermal equilibrium. That is why everything in the room ends up at room temperature.

SI units and the kelvin

Many attempts were made to measure relative temperature; the first widely accepted scale was introduced by the Polish-born Dutch physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit.

The kelvin is the base unit of temperature in the International System of Units (SI). There are seven base units and all other units are derived from them:

QuantityBase unit
masskilogram (kg)
lengthmetre (m)
timesecond (s)
electric currentampere (A)
temperaturekelvin (K)
amount of substancemole (mol) (Structure 1.4)
luminous intensitycandela (cd)
MeasurementMaking, recording and communicating measurements benefits from agreed scales. The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM, Bureau international des poids et mesures), set up in the late 19th century, is an international organisation that sets up and continually refines measurement standards and keeps the use of SI units uniform around the world. The SI (Système international d'unités) is the most used system. All other units are derived from the seven base units, e.g. volume (m³), density (kg m⁻³), energy (joule, J, where 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻²). The base units are defined by seven constants, including the Boltzmann constant k, the speed of light c, the Avogadro constant NA and the Planck constant h. Universal, precisely defined units let scientists in different countries understand each other and share results. Question: what other advantages do shared, updated measurement systems have? (Look up the Mars Climate Orbiter, lost because one team used imperial units and another metric units.) A platinum–iridium cylinder kept in France (with copies in other countries, such as the US) used to define the kilogram; it became obsolete in 2019 when the kilogram and all other SI units were redefined as exact quantities based on physical constants.
ATL Thinking skillsSeveral temperature scales have been developed, each with different reference points (table 4).
ScaleDateReference points
Newton1700sH₂O freezing point = 0°; human body temperature = 12°
Fahrenheit1700sH₂O freezing point = 32°; H₂O boiling point = 212°
Delisle1700sH₂O freezing point = 150°; H₂O boiling point = 0°
Celsius1700sH₂O freezing point = 0°; H₂O boiling point = 100°
Kelvin1800sabsolute zero = 0
CGPM1950striple point of water = 273.16 K
BIPM2018kelvin defined in terms of the Boltzmann constant, k
Temperature is related to thermal energy and could be expressed in joules (defined from kg, m and s), but the kelvin was kept as an SI base unit "for historical and practical reasons". What might these be? Using table 4: identify one thing you see, one thing it makes you think about, and one thing it makes you wonder.

Absolute zero and the Celsius–Kelvin relationship

Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of particles and is an absolute scale. In the lab we measure in degrees Celsius, but we convert to kelvin for calculations (gas laws, energetics, kinetics). On the Kelvin scale there are no negative values, so doubling the kelvin temperature really does double the average kinetic energy, which is not true in °C.

Absolute zero (0 K): particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy and cannot transfer any kinetic energy on collisions. Matter at absolute zero cannot lose heat and so cannot get any colder. It is a theoretical limit: it can be approached but never quite reached, and negative kelvin temperatures are impossible.

  • An increase of 1 K equals an increase of 1 °C, so a change in temperature is the same in both scales.
  • 0 °C = 273.15 K. Water boils at 100 °C = 373.15 K (normal pressure).
  • Absolute zero = −273.15 °C.
T / K = T / °C + 273.15T / °C = T / K − 273.15
Reference pointCelsiusKelvin
water boils100 °C373 K
human body37 °C310 K
room temperature25 °C298 K
water freezes0 °C273 K
dry ice (solid CO₂)−78 °C195 K
liquid air−191 °C82 K
absolute zero−273 °C0 K

Values in this table are rounded to whole numbers. Kinetic energy of particles is covered further in Reactivity 2.2.

Exam tip · kelvinT(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 (273 is usually accepted). A change in temperature is the same in both scales: 22 °C → 36 °C is a change of 14 °C and of 14 K. Absolute zero (0 K) is the theoretical temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy, so negative kelvin values are impossible.

Convert 25 °C to kelvin.

T / K = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15 K (298 K is accepted).

A substance warms from 22 °C to 36 °C. What is the temperature change in kelvin?

ΔT = 36 − 22 = 14 °C. The degree and the kelvin are the same size, so ΔT = 14 K. Do not add 273 to a temperature change.

Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. What is this in °C (to the nearest degree)?

T / °C = 77 − 273.15 = −196.15, so −196 °C.

Particles in a sample do not all have the same energy

Temperature is an average. At any moment, some particles are moving slowly and some very fast. A graph of the number of particles against their kinetic energy, for a sample at 298 K, rises steeply from zero, reaches a peak (the most common energy) and then tails off slowly towards high energies without ever quite reaching zero.

  • The total area under the curve represents the total number of particles.
  • The area beyond a certain energy (often shaded) is the number of particles that have at least that much energy, for example enough energy to react if they collide.
  • At a higher temperature the peak moves to higher energy and becomes lower and broader, but the area stays the same (same number of particles). More particles are now in the high-energy tail.

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide, with enough energy, and in the correct orientation. Raising the temperature increases the proportion of particles with enough energy, which is why reactions go faster when heated (Reactivity 2.2).

A sample of gas is heated from 298 K to 350 K. What happens to its energy distribution curve?

  1. The peak moves to lower energy and the area increases
  2. The peak moves to higher energy and the curve flattens; the area stays the same
  3. The whole curve moves upwards
  4. Nothing, because the number of particles is unchanged

Same number of particles, so the same area. Higher average kinetic energy shifts the peak right, and the spread of energies widens, so the peak is lower.

Linking questionsWhat is the graphical distribution of kinetic energy values of particles in a sample at a fixed temperature? (Reactivity 2.2) What must happen to particles for a chemical reaction to occur? (Reactivity 2.2)

Before you start the end-of-topic questions

These end-of-topic questions cover all of Structure 1.1: elements, compounds and mixtures, separation techniques, states of matter and changes of state, heating curves and the Kelvin scale. Before attempting them, make sure you can classify a substance as an element, compound, homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture; choose and describe a separation method (filtration, evaporation, crystallization, distillation, chromatography, magnet); name the six changes of state and say whether each is endothermic or exothermic; explain the flat sections of a heating curve; and convert between °C and K using T / K = T / °C + 273.15, remembering that Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of particles.

Kelvin temperature is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles, and the lowest possible temperature, 0 K, is called absolute zero.
